extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, and inventors preparing patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing when multiple inventions, machines, processes, products, combinations, sub-combinations, or elements may be joined in a single patent application or must be divided into separate applications. Focuses on the Patent Office's stricter rules (dependency/inseparability, combination doctrine, generic/species distinctions, and process/apparatus/product relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate and independent inventions cannot be joined
rubrics_metrics.description: Their design and operation being independent of each other there is no point of view from which they can be considered as one invention; patents embracing two or more such inventions will not be sustained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventions are separate, independent, and not connected in nature, design, or operation, a division should be demanded (cases: McComb v. Brodie; Ex parte Heginbotham; Sessions v. Rodman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions appropriate for use in the same article for common purpose may be joined
rubrics_metrics.description: That inventions appropriate for use in the same article for a common purpose of making the article may be joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts permit joinder when devices are kindred, used together, or serve a common end (e.g., Maxheimer v. Meyer; Ex parte Noyes). Patent Office still examines dependency and unity of result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related inventions invented by different inventors cannot be joined
rubrics_metrics.description: Related inventions, if invented by different inventors, cannot be joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joinder in one application presupposes common inventive ownership; separate inventors' related inventions should be separate (see Potter v. Wilson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office rule: join only where one invention is dependent on the other producing a single result
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office permits the joinder of distinct inventions in an application where one of such inventions is dependent on the other and where they thus mutually contribute to produce a single result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependency means that one invention cannot be contemplated as complete or operative except with the other (see Ex parte Young). If inventions directly act together to produce the resultant operation, joinder may be proper (Ex parte Herr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry: are included inventions independent or kindred/auxiliary?
rubrics_metrics.description: First inquiry is whether inventions included can reasonably and properly be said to be independent inventions — if independent and separate, they should not be joined; if kindred and auxiliary or connected in design/operation, division ordinarily should not be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should evaluate scope and relation of concrete inventions, not merely unity of inventor's mental conception (Ex parte Young; Ex parte Freese).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inseparability/Dependence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions are 'inseparable' whenever either one of them is necessarily dependent on the other — e.g., a product which can be created only by a specific process is inseparable from that process; an apparatus with no other use than in performing the art may be inseparable from that art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependence is determined by whether the ultimate end for which one was created cannot be reached without the other, whether one results in production of the other, or whether the use of one involves concurrent use of the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: No joinder where inventions do not co-operate in function or result
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions which co-operate neither in function nor in result cannot be joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the parts do not mutually contribute to a unitary result, the Patent Office will require division (Ex parte Westcott).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination doctrine: principal combination links sub-combinations/elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination, its sub-combinations, and the elements of each sub-combination are dependent inventions whenever such elements and sub-combinations are considered in reference to the principal combination in which all unite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the principal combination is the subject-matter of the application, subordinate elements and sub-combinations (if invented by the applicant and not previously patented) may be joined in the same application. Absent the principal combination, subordinate members are governed by general joinder rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different combinations/sub-combinations may be separately claimed if new and useful
rubrics_metrics.description: If several combinations of elements are new and useful and will severally produce new and useful results, the inventor is entitled to a patent for the several combinations, provided he files written descriptions for each and complies with the Patent Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such combinations can be claimed in one specification with separate claims, avoiding the need for separate applications (Stevens v. Pritchard; Banks v. Snediker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements in general use cannot be joined with a combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements already in general use in other connections cannot be joined with the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an element lacks novelty or utility in the relevant context (already known in the arts), the Patent Office may refuse joinder with a claimed combination (Ex parte LaBorde).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic and species claims — when genus + species can be joined
rubrics_metrics.description: A discoverer of a genus may claim broadly; a generic invention and one species under the genus may be joined; but two distinct species under the same genus requiring different inventive acts cannot be joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When substitution of one form for another involves invention, the differences are patentable as distinct species; if substitution requires only mechanical skill (no inventive act), then differences are mere modifications of a single species (Ex parte Kook; Ex parte Howland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office stricter than courts on joining arts/processes/apparatus/products
rubrics_metrics.description: The special rules for joinder of arts or processes with each other or with related inventions of different classes are more stringent in the Patent Office than in the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts permit broader joinder when related to a common end; Patent Office scrutinizes separability and unity of invention because of classification and examination workload (contrast cases cited throughout §473).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process vs apparatus: separability determines separate patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a process can be performed by different apparatus, it is separately patentable from the apparatus which performs it. Where an apparatus can be used for no other purpose than performing the process, the process may be the mere function of the apparatus and separability is affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If process can exist apart from one specific apparatus, claim process separately; if apparatus is inseparable (performs process exclusively), joinder may be proper but must be examined for dependence (Gage v. Kellogg; Ex parte Tyne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process and apparatus may be joined only when inseparable or constitute combination-process
rubrics_metrics.description: Either one must be in its own nature dependent on the other, or together they must constitute a combination-process which is also made the subject-matter of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process cannot be joined with a machine merely because they relate to the same subject; they must be inseparably connected in function/result (Gage v. Kellogg; Ex parte McDougall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process and product: join only if inseparable and fully described
rubrics_metrics.description: A process and its product may be joined if inseparable; when joined each must be fully described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts sometimes allow joinder if inventor had both results in mind. Patent Office requires inseparability or requisite unity and full disclosure of each (Welling v. Rubber Coated Harness; Belleher v. Darling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine and its integral parts or machine/product/process: join when existence is mutually dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Machines and their integral parts, a machine and the product it produces, or a machine and the process it performs, are proper subjects for a single patent when either cannot exist as a concrete and practical invention without the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office rules require separate applications for different machines unless one cannot be contemplated as operative without the other, or they are elements/sub-combinations of a principal machine (Wheeler v. McCormick; Ex parte Bigelow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate claims required when joinder covers multiple inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may include several inventions in one specification, but separate claims must be filed to secure exclusive rights to each separate combination or invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventor may describe multiple combinations in one specification and make separate claims referring to that description, avoiding multiple applications; omission of claims may jeopardize rights (Stevens v. Pritchard; Clifford discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: No joinder unless inventions directly act in producing resultant operation
rubrics_metrics.description: No joinder is permitted in the Patent Office unless the inventions directly act in producing a resultant operation due to all the inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must determine that the inventions co-act (co-operate) toward a single operative result; mere relation to same subject or genus is insufficient (Ex parte Herr; Ex parte Sol Kuh).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregated devices or distinct species under same genus often require division
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregated devices cannot be joined unless the joinder would be proper when they are considered as distinct inventions; two distinct species under the same genus that require different inventive acts cannot be joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where aggregation produces distinct inventions or where species are patentably distinct, separate patents or divisionals should be required (Ex parte Cardwell; Ex parte Ewart; Ex parte Dinkelbuehler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office discretion: Patent Office decides separability and distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is for the Patent Office to judge whether inventions are separate and distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office applies its regulations and case law to balance examination practicality, classification, and the statutory requirements; many cited Ex parte decisions illustrate this discretion.
